This report provides findings regarding the size and scale and profile of private sector artificial intelligence ( AI ) business activity in the UK in 2025.
50 in-depth interviews with AI businesses, academic and policy stakeholders, and investors
an estimated 130,400 people were employed in AI -related roles, an increase of 51% on 2024
AI -related revenues increased by 41% to £33.6 billion, with revenues among dedicated AI companies almost doubling to £9.2 billion
AI -related gross value added ( GVA ) increased by 58% to £18.6 billion, including a more than doubling of GVA among dedicated AI companies to £4.8 billion
A total of 10,488 AI companies were identified, up 79% on 2024. While some of this increase reflected improved coverage and the growing prominence of AI in how companies describe their products and services, it is underpinned by genuine market expansion.
Approximately 1,750 new AI companies were incorporated in 2025 alone, and 186 large companies entered the scope of the study across a broader range of sectors than in previous years. The balance of the sector shifted towards dedicated AI companies (68%, up from 56% in 2024), pointing to a wave of small, AI -native market entrants and a ‘doubling down’ on AI as a core business driver.
The sector’s economic contribution grew strongly across all headline measures. AI -related revenues increased by 41% to £33.6 billion in 2025, with growth more balanced between companies that have AI products and services as their core focus, and those that have AI activity as part of a broader business offer (referred to as dedicated and diversified companies) than in previous years.
Dedicated company revenues almost doubled (from £4.9 billion to £9.2 billion), accounting for 44% of total revenue growth. An estimated 130,400 people were employed in AI -related roles (+51% compared to 2024), with companies identified in the 2024 study increasing AI -related headcount by 31% on a like-for-like basis.
AI -related GVA reached £18.6 billion (+58%). Large companies continued to generate the majority of AI -related revenue (82%), although the SME share rose from 15% to 18%.
Despite notable increases in fundraising evidenced in this study, firms reported that access to capital remained the most significant constraint on growth. Access to equity investment was the barrier most commonly cited as significantly affecting businesses’ ability to meet their goals (61% of survey respondents).
The availability of scale-up funding was the factor most commonly expected to significantly affect future AI activity (57%), and the most commonly cited potential reason for relocating activity away from the UK. Competition for experienced AI talent, and visa and immigration barriers, remain prominent concerns.
Access to computing power became a more significant issue than in previous years. For example, 72% of surveyed businesses reported an increased compute requirement over the past 12 months (up from 66% of businesses in 2024).
91% of those using compute expect costs to rise, with energy costs and grid connections identified as the underlying constraints on UK AI infrastructure. Lack of regulatory clarity was cited as a significant barrier by 25% of businesses (up from 16% in 2024).
Fundraising by dedicated AI companies more than doubled to £6.3 billion in 2025. Growth was driven at both ends of the investment market. Rounds of £100 million or more accounted for around 60% of 2025 investment value, with 2 companies accounting for almost half of all funds raised since the start of 2025, while record numbers of companies secured investment for the first time.
More than 1 in 4 dedicated AI companies raised external investment since 2020. Inward investment also strengthened, with 79 AI -related foreign direct investment ( FDI ) projects announced or opened in 2025, associated with an estimated $8.9 billion of capital investment and approximately 8,600 expected jobs.
However, qualitative evidence indicates a ‘bifurcated’ funding environment. Very large sums are reaching a small number of infrastructure and frontier companies, while many application-layer businesses report a much tougher fundraising climate.
AI activity remained concentrated in London, the South East, and the East of England, which together accounted for 72% of registered office locations. However, the sector’s operational footprint extends further across the UK’s nations and regions, with distinct regional specialisms evident (for example, life sciences in the East of England and autonomous systems in Scotland). Approximately 1 in 7 AI companies operated from more than one UK location.
The sector is increasingly international. 1,372 internationally headquartered AI companies now operate in the UK (13% of the total, of which 54% are US-headquartered), while more than 1 in 5 UK-headquartered AI companies maintains at least one overseas location, spanning 4,805 locations across 136 countries.
Interviewees continued to place the UK among the leading AI nations, in line with qualitative evidence from previous studies, but cited growing pressure from heavily investing states. Dependence on a small number of overseas (predominantly US) technology providers emerged as a key theme.
47% of surveyed businesses import AI products or services, and 38% of importers described themselves as entirely dependent on them. However, few interviewees advocated full self-sufficiency.
Instead, the prevailing view favoured diversification (including greater use of open-source models), securing the UK’s data assets, and targeted investment in sovereign capability, with AI model efficiency and specialised applications seen as the UK’s most practical competitive response.
The qualitative research provided additional depth on how AI businesses experienced the market conditions described elsewhere in the main report.

The findings should be taken as contextual evidence that helps explain the reasons behind business views, rather than as representative measures of the wider UK AI sector.
Across the interviews, businesses described a sector with strong innovation potential, but where growth depended on a set of interconnected market conditions.
A recurring theme was the distinction between starting and scaling an AI business in the UK. The UK was viewed as a positive environment for founding AI companies, supported by strong research capability, entrepreneurial activity, and a growing pool of AI firms. However, businesses were more cautious about the UK’s ability to support later-stage growth.
Qualitative insight boxes like these throughout the report present findings from Ipsos qualitative interviews with 30 AI businesses. Findings reflect the views and experiences of participating businesses and are not intended to be representative of the wider UK AI sector or the views of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade ( BIST ) or the UK government.
The authors would like to thank members of the BIST team for their input throughout the study. BIST and the report authors would also like to thank all those who contributed to the research. This includes those who took part in strategic stakeholder interviews, responded to the business survey, or otherwise offered evidence and insights to the study.
Perspective Economics, in collaboration with Beauhurst, Ipsos, and a consortium of advisors was commissioned in February 2026 to deliver an analysis of the UK’s artificial intelligence ( AI ) sector in 2025.
The aim of the study is to continue building a better understanding of the scale, profile and economic contribution of the UK’s AI sector by updating previous data compiled since 2022. This is to support the government’s ongoing development and monitoring of key AI policies.
In addition to providing updated economic data, this report offers insights from UK AI businesses and stakeholders regarding the ongoing opportunities, challenges, enablers, and barriers to the continued growth of AI activity in the UK.
This study forms part of the broader BIST evidence base on AI , building on similar studies conducted since 2022. The study has several overarching objectives as follows:
Draw on a comprehensive range of data sources to identify and document UK AI companies.
Conduct qualitative research to understand a range of issues including UK AI company collaboration, sector challenges, growth opportunities, and enablers.
Produce AI sector demographics and economic estimates.
Use qualitative and quantitative research findings to produce thematic analysis, including analysis of UK market dynamics and competition.
Develop scenarios based on findings regarding UK market dynamics and competition and their implications for UK AI economic activity.
A list of research questions that informed the design of the study is available in the report appendices.
The study used a mixed methods approach, combining desk-based review, qualitative and quantitative research and analysis.
A multi-modal survey of AI firms was conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, returning 376 responses. A total of 50 in-depth interviews were completed with businesses (30), academic and policy stakeholders (10), and investors (10).
A majority of interviews were conducted between April and May 2026, with a small number completed in June according to stakeholder availability. A regional expert advisory panel was also convened to test emerging findings.
The baseline company dataset was reviewed and updated between March and June 2026, with the research team identifying, verifying, and enriching UK-registered firms with evidence of AI -related commercial activity.
In total, 10,488 unique active firms were included in the study, informing sector estimates for revenue, employment, and GVA .
The identification and analysis of firms followed 7 stages, set out in full in Appendix 4.
A review of AI -related literature, announcements, and investment activity (January 2025 to March 2026) to ground the analysis, update AI -related key terms, and identify new sources for review.
Identification of potentially relevant firms across a wide range of official, commercial, and web-based sources.
Workshops with BIST to test the study scope and definitions, and to update the AI taxonomy against market developments while maintaining comparability with previous studies.
Automated and manual checks verifying each firm’s web presence, registered entity, and activity, with structured review of web content to evidence AI -related products and services, and removal of duplicates, dormant entities, and non-commercial organisations.
The Ipsos survey, in-depth stakeholder interviews, and regional expert advisory panel noted.
Final additions and verification checks (June 2026), including newly registered firms and firms coming out of ‘stealth’, resulting in the final study population.
Estimation of AI -related employment, revenue, and GVA for each firm, using known accounts where available and conservative estimation for unknown values, aggregated for sector-level analysis.
Key data sources used in this iteration of the study are summarised in Table 1.1.
Artificial intelligence activity in the UK is not defined by a formal Standard Industrial Classification ( SIC ) code. This study therefore uses experimental methods to identify and quantify AI activity across traditional economic sectors.
The approach and methodology are consistent with those employed to deliver analyses of the UK cyber security sector annually since 2018, and with the method used to create baseline evidence regarding the AI sector since 2022.
The data used to inform the study includes identification of AI firms according to a taxonomy developed and agreed with academic experts and BIST , applied using multiple corroborating sources. This includes review of websites, news, and official sources supported by large language models ( LLMs ), subject to manual validation and review throughout.
Enrichment of web data using open and proprietary data sources were also used to used to inform the study, including:
Companies House (company name, registration number, locations, incorporation date)
Bureau van Dijk FAME (revenue, employment, profitability, remuneration, research and development ( R&D ) spend)
Beauhurst (external grants, fundraisings, accelerator attendance, M&A activity)
The estimates within this study are experimental in nature and do not constitute official statistics. All figures reflect a best estimate at a point in time (final checks were undertaken in June 2026).
Only a small proportion of firms file full detailed accounts with directly observable revenue and GVA . For the remainder, values are modelled using per-employee estimates applied to estimated AI -related employment, calibrated against anonymised survey responses and baseline data.
Estimates are therefore best used to indicate the broad size, scale, and composition of the sector, and to compare relative contributions across sub-sectors, regions, and firm sizes rather than as precise values, particularly at the level of individual firms.
Quality assurance was applied at each stage of the research, combining automated checks with manual review, with final decisions on ‘edge’ cases made by the research team using expert review, and with the study scope, taxonomy, and emerging findings reviewed with BIST and the regional expert advisory panel.
The full research methodology, including quality assurance and research limitations, is set out in Appendix 4.
This study builds on the previous AI sectoral analyses. [footnote 9] It uses the same approach and methodology to identify AI companies and produce headline sector estimates of revenue, employment, and GVA .
As the sector continues to evolve, so do the analytical parameters used to produce lower-level analyses of the sector. The study team worked with BIST representatives and external experts to update the taxonomy used to categorise the sector. This has evolved from 3 key business models and 7 high-level capability domains to a more detailed multi-level framework within this iteration of the study. This year’s taxonomy is included in Section 2 of the report, with explanations regarding key changes.
The tools and language used to identify AI firms also continue to develop. We note that year-on-year changes reflect both ongoing methodological improvement and widening terminology, as well as genuine market growth, and comparisons over time should be interpreted accordingly (see Appendix 4).
The following updates have been made to the research methodology.
The study context has been updated to reflect market and policy developments since the previous report, informed by a desk-based review of AI -related literature, announcements, and investment activity covering January 2025 to March 2026 (see Stage 1).
The identification, enrichment, and classification of firms has been undertaken in-house by the research team, supporting greater consistency, quality assurance, and comparability with the previous baseline dataset.
The research team has continued to innovate and improve processes for capturing, triaging, and reviewing web data at scale, strengthening the evidence base used to assess each firm’s AI -related products and services.
All firms are tagged against the updated taxonomy using multiple corroborating sources (such as web content, company accounts, investment activity, and employment signals), rather than reliance upon any single source.
Additional sources have been incorporated within the longlisting process (inward investment, trade, public procurement, and publicly funded research data) to support the identification of relevant firms (see Stage 2).
The research team has continued to make use of leading LLMs and agentic web research tooling to support the review, verification, and classification of firms, subject to manual validation and quality review throughout. This enables analysis of company data at a rapid scale that would not be possible by human review alone, while preserving review and human-in-the-loop checks.
Automated checks are combined with manual review at each stage of the process, with final decisions regarding ‘edge’ cases undertaken by the research team using expert review.
The study is supported by a survey of 376 AI firms and 50 in-depth stakeholder interviews, expanding the firm-level and qualitative evidence base relative to previous studies.
A regional expert advisory panel was convened to test emerging findings, provide challenge regarding regional coverage and interpretation, and identify firms or initiatives for further consideration.
The following sub-sections provide further information regarding the approach and methodology used to produce the study, including scoping and definitions, data sources and research limitations. It also provides a note about how the estimates provided in the study should be read and interpreted.
This study provides an estimate of the size and scale of AI activity in the UK, continuing the time-series analysis undertaken since 2022. AI activity is not captured by a SIC code, and the study therefore adopts an experimental approach, combining, analysing and estimating using a range of official, commercial, and web-based sources.
have a clear presence within the UK market, through a UK-registered business that reports to Companies House
demonstrate an active provision of commercial activity related to AI (for example, via website or social media content)
provide AI products or services to the market (for example, sell or enable the selling of AI products or services, rather than simply adopting AI tools)
appear to be active at the time of writing – charities, universities, networks, and individual (non-registered) contractors are excluded
The study includes internationally headquartered firms with an evidenced UK trading presence. All economic estimates relate to UK activity only (for example, revenue reported within UK entities, UK-based employment, and GVA ).
Firms are classified as dedicated (typically smaller, specialised AI -first companies) or diversified (typically larger companies with an AI offer alongside a broader business). For dedicated firms, all UK activity is included within sector estimates, and for diversified firms, only the estimated AI -related share is included in the sector estimates.
The study draws upon multiple complementary sources.
Companies House data and filed accounts (via Bureau van Dijk FAME ), used to verify registered entities and to provide employment, revenue and GVA data
HMRC Trade Info, providing a supporting signal of trading activity
the UKRI Gateway to Research, identifying firms engaged in publicly funded AI -related research
Beauhurst, used to identify external investment raised (dedicated firms only)
Lightcast and anonymised web profiles, used to identify AI -related employment and estimate the AI -related share of activity within diversified firms
fDi Markets, identifying announced inward investment
Tussell, identifying AI -related public procurement
Company websites and wider web content collated by Perspective Economics, used to identify firms, evidence their AI -related products and services, and classify each firm against the agreed taxonomy.
A multi-modal survey of 376 AI firms (conducted by Ipsos, May 2026), used to understand firm-level performance and perceptions and to calibrate modelled estimates (for example, pre-revenue firms); and 50 in-depth interviews with stakeholders across industry, academia, government policy and investment.
In bringing these sources together, the research team combined a range of analytical tools (including LLMs ) with manual review at each stage, with the evidence and rationale underpinning each classification recorded within the final dataset.
The approach and emerging findings were also reviewed with BIST and a regional expert advisory panel throughout. Further detail on quality assurance is set out in the methodology annex. We note this dataset and analysis have been developed for research purposes only.
There is no single agreed definition of what constitutes the AI ‘sector’, and its boundaries are rightly contested. Identification relies on definitional scoping and review of web and trading data, and determination of AI firms in scope represents a best estimate by the research team against agreed parameters, rather than a definitive classification.
Further, the line between firms that develop value-adding AI products and services and those that adopt AI is increasingly difficult to draw, particularly among diversified firms. However, all firms have been reviewed with regard to evidence of providing an AI -related product or service to the market.
The tools and techniques used to identify and classify firms have improved considerably since the first analysis in 2022, while the language of AI as a technology and as a sector continues to broaden.
Year-on-year changes therefore reflect both ongoing methodological improvement and widening scope, as well as genuine market growth, and should be interpreted with that in mind. The research sets out time-series analysis accordingly.
Where values are not available via filed accounts, revenue, GVA , and AI -related employment are estimated or modelled on a per-employee basis, with ‘conservative’ low-end estimates applied for unknown values (see methodology in full).
Identification of products, services and capabilities is informed by review of descriptive web content, where the extent of a firm’s self-reported AI activity can vary. This has been subject to quality review.
Survey and interview findings rely upon voluntary engagement and may not fully represent the wider population of AI firms.
The study reflects a dynamic market, with final checks undertaken in June 2026. Many of the data sources (such as accounts) may vary in time reported but typically reflect the most recent year of trading.
A fuller statement of the research scope and limitations is set out in the methodology annex.
The estimates within this study are experimental in nature and do not constitute official statistics. All figures reflect a best estimate at a point in time (final checks were undertaken in June 2026), derived from multiple official, commercial, and web-based sources.
Only a small proportion of firms file full detailed accounts with directly observable revenue and GVA . For the remainder, values are modelled using conservative per-employee estimates applied to estimated AI -related employment, calibrated against anonymised survey responses (including pre-revenue firms).
Where activity cannot be reliably verified (for example, recently incorporated firms yet to file accounts), null values are applied rather than imputed estimates. Reported revenue and GVA figures should therefore be regarded as a conservative estimate of AI -related activity.
Estimates are best used to indicate the broad size, scale, and composition of the sector, and to compare relative contributions across sub-sectors, regions, and firm sizes rather than as precise values, particularly at the level of individual firms.
